{{Short description|Type of object in algebraic geometry}}

In [[algebraic geometry]], a '''Deligne–Mumford stack''' is a [[stack (mathematics)|stack]] that behaves, in many respects, like an [[algebraic variety]] or an [[orbifold]], while still allowing mild stacky phenomena such as finite stabilizer groups. More precisely, a stack <math>F</math> over schemes is Deligne–Mumford if its diagonal is sufficiently well behaved and if it admits an [[étale morphism|étale]] surjective cover by a scheme (an ''atlas'').<ref name="StacksDM">{{Citation
 | title = The Stacks project
 | publisher = The Stacks Project Authors
 | url = https://stacks.math.columbia.edu
 | chapter = Deligne–Mumford stacks
}}</ref>

[[Pierre Deligne]] and [[David Mumford]] introduced this notion in their 1969 paper on the irreducibility of the [[moduli space of algebraic curves]], where they showed that the moduli stack of stable curves of fixed [[arithmetic genus]] is a proper smooth Deligne–Mumford stack over <math>\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Z}</math>.<ref name="DM1969">{{Citation
 | last1 = Deligne | first1 = Pierre | author1-link = Pierre Deligne
 | last2 = Mumford | first2 = David | author2-link = David Mumford
 | title = The irreducibility of the space of curves of given genus
 | journal = Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS
 | volume = 36 | year = 1969 | issue = 1
 | pages = 75–109
 | url = https://www.numdam.org/item?id=PMIHES_1969__36__75_0
 | doi = 10.1007/BF02684599
 | mr = 0262240
| url-access = subscription
 }}</ref> Since then, Deligne–Mumford stacks have become a basic tool in moduli theory and in modern [[intersection theory]], for instance in [[Gromov–Witten invariant|Gromov–Witten theory]].<ref>{{Citation
 | last = Fantechi | first = Barbara
 | title = Stacks for everybody
 | journal = Notices of the American Mathematical Society
 | year = 2003
 | url = https://www.ams.org/notices/200304/what-is.pdf
}}</ref>

== Definition ==

Let <math>S</math> be a base scheme, and let ''F'' be a stack on <math>(\operatorname{Sch}/S)_{\text{ét}}</math>. The stack ''F'' is called a '''Deligne–Mumford stack''' if the following conditions hold:<ref name="StacksDM" />

# The diagonal morphism <math display="block">\Delta_F\colon F \to F \times_S F</math> is [[representable morphism of stacks|representable]], quasi-compact and separated.
# There exists a scheme ''U'' and a representable, surjective, [[étale morphism|étale]] morphism <math display="block">U \to F,</math> called an ''atlas'' (or ''cover'') of ''F''.

Many authors formulate the definition in the context of algebraic stacks by additionally requiring that ''F'' be an [[algebraic stack]] (in the sense of [[Michael Artin]]). In such formulations, a Deligne–Mumford stack is an algebraic stack whose diagonal is unramified and which admits an étale surjective atlas by a scheme.<ref>{{Citation
 | last = Laumon | first = Gérard |author-link=Gérard Laumon
 | last2 = Moret-Bailly | first2 = Laurent
 | title = Champs algébriques
 | series = Ergebnisse der Mathematik und ihrer Grenzgebiete
 | volume = 39
 | publisher = Springer-Verlag
 | year = 2000
 | mr = 1771927
}}</ref>

== Relation with other notions ==

=== Algebraic stacks and Artin stacks ===

If, in the definition above, the word “étale” is weakened to “[[smooth morphism|smooth]]”, one obtains the notion of an '''algebraic stack''' (often called an '''Artin stack''' after Michael Artin). Thus every Deligne–Mumford stack is an algebraic (Artin) stack, but not conversely.<ref name="FantechiStacks">{{Citation
 | last = Fantechi | first = Barbara
 | title = Stacks for everybody
 | journal = European Congress of Mathematics (Barcelona, 2000)
 | publisher = Birkhäuser
 | year = 2001
 | pages = 329–349
}}</ref>

The condition that the atlas is étale forces stabilizer groups to be [[finite group|finite]] and unramified over the base. In contrast, general Artin stacks may have positive-dimensional stabilizers, such as copies of <math>\mathbb{G}_m</math> or [[abelian variety|abelian varieties]].<ref name="StacksDM" />

=== Algebraic spaces ===

An [[algebraic space]] can be regarded as a special case of a Deligne–Mumford stack, namely a Deligne–Mumford stack whose diagonal is an [[Immersion (mathematics)|immersion]] and whose stabilizer groups are trivial. In this sense, algebraic spaces are “non-stacky” Deligne–Mumford stacks.<ref>{{Citation
 | title = The Stacks project
 | publisher = The Stacks Project Authors
 | url = https://stacks.math.columbia.edu
 | chapter = Algebraic spaces
}}</ref>

=== Orbifolds ===

Over the complex numbers, separated Deligne–Mumford stacks of finite type with finite stabilizers are often viewed as algebro-geometric analogues of [[orbifold]]s. More precisely, a smooth Deligne–Mumford stack over <math>\mathbb{C}</math> with finite stabilizers determines, and is determined by, a complex orbifold together with additional algebro-geometric structure.<ref>{{Citation
 | title = Deligne–Mumford stack
 | work = nLab
 | url = https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Deligne-Mumford%2Bstack
 | access-date = 2025-11-14
}}</ref>

== Properties ==

Let ''F'' be a Deligne–Mumford stack that is quasi-compact and quasi-separated.

* '''Finite stabilizers and automorphisms.''' For any quasi-compact scheme ''B'' and any object <math>X \in F(B)</math>, the automorphism group of ''X'' over ''B'' is finite. Equivalently, the [[inertia stack]] of ''F'' is finite over ''F''.<ref name="StacksDM" />
* '''Coarse moduli spaces.''' If the inertia stack of ''F'' is finite (for example, if ''F'' is a separated Deligne–Mumford stack locally of finite type over a Noetherian base), then ''F'' admits a [[coarse moduli space]] in the sense of Deligne–Mumford, which is an algebraic space representing isomorphism classes of objects up to finite stabilizers.<ref>{{Citation
 | last = Rydh | first = David
 | title = Existence of quotients by finite groups and coarse moduli spaces
 | journal = Annales de l'Institut Fourier
 | volume = 58
 | year = 2008
 | pages = 531–559
 | url = https://people.kth.se/~dary/quotients20070712.pdf
}}</ref><ref name="StacksDM" />

* '''Presentation by groupoids.''' Every Deligne–Mumford stack ''F'' admits a presentation by a [[groupoid]] in schemes. Concretely, if ''U'' → ''F'' is an étale surjective atlas, then the fiber product <math>R = U \times_F U</math> defines a [[groupoid scheme]] <math>R \rightrightarrows U</math> whose associated quotient stack is equivalent to ''F''. See [[groupoid scheme]] for details.<ref name="StacksDM" />
* '''Local quotient structure.''' Étale-locally on the base, a Deligne–Mumford stack is a quotient of a scheme by a finite group action: for every point of ''F'' there is an étale neighborhood over which ''F'' is equivalent to a quotient stack <math>[X/G]</math> with ''G'' finite (often referred to as an ''orbifold chart'').<ref>{{Citation
 | title = The Stacks project
 | publisher = The Stacks Project Authors
 | url = https://stacks.math.columbia.edu
 | chapter = Quotient stacks
}}</ref><ref>{{Citation
 | last = Alper | first = Jarod
 | title = A guide to the literature on algebraic stacks
 | journal = Handbook of Moduli, Vol. I
 | publisher = International Press
 | year = 2013
 | pages = 527–583
 | url = https://maths-people.anu.edu.au/~alperj/papers/stacks-guide.pdf
}}</ref>

== Examples ==

=== Quotient by a finite group (affine stacks) ===

A basic way to construct Deligne–Mumford stacks is to take the [[stack quotient]] of a scheme or algebraic space by a finite group action with finite stabilizers. Let
<math>
C_n = \langle a \mid a^n = 1 \rangle
</math>
be a [[cyclic group]] of order ''n'' acting on <math>\mathbb{C}^2</math> by
<math display="block">
a\cdot(x,y) = (\zeta_n x,\;\zeta_n y),
</math>
where <math>\zeta_n</math> is a primitive ''n''th [[root of unity]]. The quotient stack
<math>[\mathbb{C}^2 / C_n]</math>
is then an affine smooth Deligne–Mumford stack: the stabilizer is trivial away from the origin, and equal to the full group at the origin, so all stabilizers are finite.

More generally, if a finite group ''G'' acts on a scheme ''X'' over a base scheme ''S'' in such a way that the action is étale and the stabilizers are finite over ''S'', then the quotient stack <math>[X/G]</math> is a Deligne–Mumford stack over ''S''.<ref name="StacksDM" /><ref>{{Citation
 | last = Edidin | first = Dan
 | title = Notes on the construction of the moduli space of curves
 | year = 1998
 | url = https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9805101
}}</ref>

=== Weighted projective stacks ===

Non-affine examples arise from [[weighted projective space]]s and weighted projective varieties. For instance, the weighted projective line <math>\mathbb{P}(2,3)</math> can be described as the quotient stack
<math>[\mathbb{C}^2 \setminus \{0\} / \mathbb{C}^*]</math>
where <math>\mathbb{C}^*</math> acts by
<math display="block">
\lambda \cdot (x,y) = (\lambda^2 x,\;\lambda^3 y).
</math>
A point <math>(x,y)</math> has a non-trivial stabilizer precisely when either <math>x = 0</math> or <math>y = 0</math>, in which case the stabilizer is a finite group of roots of unity (of order 2 or 3 respectively). Hence all stabilizers are finite and the quotient stack is Deligne–Mumford. Such stacks are sometimes referred to as ''weighted projective stacks'' or ''stacky projective lines''.<ref>{{Citation
 | last = Geigle | first = Werner
 | last2 = Lenzing | first2 = Helmut
 | title = A class of weighted projective curves arising in representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras
 | journal = Singularities, representation of algebras, and vector bundles
 | series = Lecture Notes in Mathematics
 | volume = 1273
 | publisher = Springer
 | year = 1987
 | pages = 265–297
}}</ref>

=== Moduli stacks of curves ===

The prototypical examples of Deligne–Mumford stacks arise in the [[moduli problem|moduli theory]] of curves. For an integer <math>g \geq 2</math>, the moduli stack <math>\mathcal{M}_g</math> of smooth, proper, connected curves of genus ''g'' over schemes is an algebraic stack; its Deligne–Mumford compactification <math>\overline{\mathcal{M}}_g</math>, obtained by allowing stable nodal curves, is a proper smooth Deligne–Mumford stack over <math>\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Z}</math>.<ref name="DM1969" /><ref name="StacksStableCurves">{{Citation
 | title = The Stacks project
 | publisher = The Stacks Project Authors
 | url = https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0E99
 | chapter = Properties of the stack of stable curves
}}</ref>

More generally, the moduli stacks <math>\mathcal{M}_{g,n}</math> and <math>\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n}</math> of curves of genus ''g'' with ''n'' marked points are Deligne–Mumford stacks, and their geometry plays a central role in modern enumerative geometry and intersection theory.<ref name="StacksStableCurves" /><ref>{{Citation
 | last = Schmitt | first = Johannes
 | title = The moduli space of curves
 | year = 2020
 | url = https://www.math.uni-bonn.de/~schmitt/ModCurves/Script.pdf
}}</ref>

=== Stacky curves ===

{{main|Stacky curve}}

A '''stacky curve''' is, roughly speaking, a connected, one-dimensional, separated Deligne–Mumford stack of finite type over an algebraically closed field, with generically trivial stabilizer. Such objects generalize smooth projective curves by allowing finitely many stacky points with non-trivial finite stabilizer groups. Weighted projective lines and certain orbifold curves arising in representation theory and [[arithmetic geometry]] provide basic examples.<ref>{{Citation
 | last = Abramovich | first = Dan |author-link=Dan Abramovich
 | last2 = Vistoli | first2 = Angelo |author-link2=Angelo Vistoli
 | title = Compactifying the space of stable maps
 | journal = Journal of the American Mathematical Society
 | volume = 15 | year = 2002
 | pages = 27–75
}}</ref>

== Non-example ==

A simple example of an algebraic stack that is not Deligne–Mumford is the [[classifying stack]] of the multiplicative group:
<math>
[B\mathbb{G}_m] = [\operatorname{Spec} k / \mathbb{G}_m].
</math>
Here the stabilizer group at every point is isomorphic to <math>\mathbb{G}_m</math>, which is infinite and has positive dimension. Thus the diagonal is not unramified and the stack fails to be Deligne–Mumford, although it is an Artin stack.<ref name="FantechiStacks" /><ref name="StacksDM" />
